steps.text: This chart carries one swell. It enters from the west and runs east across the whole ocean: every cell it crosses has strength, shown as a crest line.
No cell crosses another swell yet, so there are no nodes to sail by — a canoe needs crossings to travel on.
One swell alone is water without roads. Add an island, and the swell bends.
Place an island in the swell's path. Rays strike its windward face and bounce back; rays beside it bend toward it.
Where bent rays cross their own swell's neighbours, the crest lines crowd — this is a channel you can sail.
One island, one swell: the shape of the first teaching charts.
One more island, close to home, bends the swell toward your atoll and opens a launch lane.
Launch a canoe onto any strength cell beside your home atoll. Launching does not spend the canoe's sail.
Your canoe is at sea. Next: how it rides.
A canoe waits beside home. Sail east along the swell.
Each step on a swell costs one range. Steps between nodes cost none — the chain carries you.
Entering a node ends your ride unless the next cell is also a node: then the chain carries the canoe for free.
Ride the swells, stop on the nodes. That is the whole art.
The full chart: two dominant swells and two minor ones. Crossings light up everywhere — nodes are where two or more swells cross.
One island reshapes the whole sea: every ray that touches it bends or bounces, and the node field moves.
You know the field, the island, the launch, and the ride. The voyages begin.
